10146-reminiscences-of-pioneer-days-in-s:
Frank Moore gathered these reminiscences of pioneer days in St. Paul from articles written for the Daily Pioneer Press. They open with newspaper struggles of pioneer days, and a brief narration of incidents connected with the early daily newspapers of the city.

Moore imagines James M. Goodhue returning to find web-perfecting presses making twenty-five thousand impressions an hour, against the old hand press's two hundred and forty, with the linotype beside them. Readers get a newspaperman's history of a frontier city, told through its presses and its people. Moore wrote as a man who had set type himself.
10446-the-green-flag-and-other-stories-o:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathered these stories of war and sport under the title The Green Flag, with tales of soldiers, sailors, boxers, and hunters. Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, shows here his wider gift for adventure, humor, and Irish and imperial color. The stories range from barracks to boxing rings to strange catacombs.

The title tale follows Dennis Conolly, twin to a shot Irish rebel, who joins the British Army and must serve a cause he hates. Captain Sharkey, the Croxley master, and Bimbashi Joyce add pirates, sport, and empire. Readers get a vigorous, varied Doyle collection, full of action and character.
10608-the-turquoise-cup-and-the-desert:
Arthur Cosslett Smith published these two tales in 1903, opening with a cardinal archbishop on a shaded balcony, his scarlet stockings showing six inches, his hair white as spun glass. The cardinal, small and neatly made, resembles the young Napoleon, and pigeons coquet on his balcony rail. The scene sets a romantic, Mediterranean tone.

The Turquoise Cup follows the cardinal and his world of church, art, and love, while The Desert carries the reader to hotter, wilder scenes. Smith writes with color, wit, and a taste for the exotic. Readers get two elegant, early twentieth-century tales of faith, passion, and far places.
10666-the-public-vs-m-gustave-flaubert:
The Public versus M. Gustave Flaubert prints the record of the French trial that put a novelist in the dock for offending public morals and religion. The case turned on Flaubert's novel of provincial romance, and the volume opens with the speech of the prosecuting attorney, Ernest Pinard. Pinard admits the charges are vague, then argues that right-minded readers can tell when a page attacks faith and morals.

The speeches that follow lay out the whole quarrel between art and censorship in mid-nineteenth-century France. Readers get the trial itself, in the words spoken in court, rather than a later summary. It remains a key document on free expression and the novel.
11391-lectures-on-art:
Washington Allston's Lectures on Art, edited by Richard Henry Dana Jr. in 1850, collects the American painter's writings on art after his death, published ahead of a planned biography and correspondence. Dana's preface sketches Allston's life: born in Charleston, South Carolina, on November 5, 1779, schooled at Newport, Rhode Island. under Robert Rogers, entering Harvard in 1796 and graduating in 1800, developing a marked artistic talent at school and college.

Allston's lectures treat painting as a moral and intellectual art, in the manner of a learned practitioner. The volume was meant to stand beside his poems in the original design. For American art historians, it remains a key text, showing how the first major American painter theorized his craft.
1168-the-pool-in-the-desert:
Sara Jeanette Duncan knew India well, and she gathers stories set among the British there. Her people are officers, wives, and officials whose lives pool and stagnate like water in the desert heat. The title tale follows a woman caught between duty and desire in a lonely station.

Duncan writes with wit and a sharp eye for Anglo-Indian manners, gossip, and caste, both British and Indian. Her people are clever, flawed, and often lonely. The book gives a woman's view of the Raj, and it still reads as fine, unsparing short fiction.
12121-the-lady-of-the-barge-the-lady-of-:
Part 1 of W. W. Jacobs's Lady of the Barge and Other Stories opens with the title story, in which the master of the barge Arabella sits in the stern with his arm on the tiller. A desultory conversation with the mate of a schooner, hanging over his craft's side a few yards off, ends over a difference of opinion on religion.

The skipper had argued so warmly that talk broke off. Jacobs uses the barge, its crew, and the river as a stage for his short, ironic tales. The Lady of the Barge herself, and the other stories in the collection, turn on sailors' superstitions, bargains. Blunders, told in the dry, understated voice that made Jacobs a favorite humorist.
12344-sir-robert-hart:
Juliet Bredon, Sir Robert Hart niece, told The Romance of a Great Career in a second edition of 1910. Hart, an Ulsterman who became Inspector-General of the Imperial Chinese Customs, shaped China trade and revenue for nearly fifty years.

Chapters follow Hart early years, first years in China at Ningpo, the allied commission, resignation from consular service, and the beginnings of the customs service. Later chapters cover Shanghai, the Sherard Osborne affair, and appointment as inspector-general. A mid-book scene has a puzzled Hart open a brown-paper parcel with Swedish stamps, from a sender he did not know. Bredon writes with family affection and access. The book is a popular life of a remarkable imperial servant.
12570-starr-of-the-desert:
B. M. Bower's 1917 western, Starr of the Desert, opens with a commonplace man named Peter, daffodils selling at two bits a dozen beside a New York flower stand. Chapters promise a way out for Peter, a grease spot in the sand, and moonlight, a man and a song. A scientist named Holman Sommers, a dog called Pat, and a trail of Silvertown cords follow.

Starr finds something in a secret room, takes a prisoner, and watches Helen May sigh for romance and then understand. Desert, silver and mystery drive the plot, with Bower's brisk, humorous style. The novel is a light western adventure, built on mistaken identity, hidden treasure and a hero who grows into his name.
13112-speeches-from-the-dock-or-protests:
Speeches from the Dock, Part I, published in Dublin by A. M. Sullivan, gathers protests of Irish patriotism spoken after conviction. Its speakers run from Theobald Wolfe Tone and William Orr through the Sheares brothers, Robert Emmet, John Martin, William Smith O'Brien, Thomas Francis Meagher, and John Mitchel. The motto promises that freedom's battle, once begun, is ever won.

One note tells of Henry Joy McCracken, tried by court-martial at Belfast on July 17, 1798, and hanged the same evening, his prepared speech unheard by brutal judges. Another follows Terence Bellew McManus, who shaved his whiskers and slipped past spies to a ship. The book is a martyrology in the speakers' own words, fierce, mournful, and proud.
13343-the-rim-of-the-desert:
Ada Woodruff Anderson's 1915 Rim of the Desert has a frontispiece by Monte Crews. It opens with a man who never came back and a question, then moves through Snoqualmie Pass, a broken axle, apples of Eden, and the dunes of the Columbia. Anderson, author of The Strain of White, sets her tale in Alaska and the Pacific Northwest. The novel is frontier romance with a strong heroine.

A narrator recalls spending a winter on the Tanana with David Weatherbee, staking a placer, then selling out after Weatherbee sold his share to meet an obligation down in the States. Later, Banks tells how Tisdale mushed a thousand miles from Nome to the Iditarod, through fifty below and canyon winds, to reach Dave's mine. The book is a tale of grit, gold, and loyalty.
13497-greatheart:
Ethel M. Dell's 1918 novel Greatheart takes its motto from Pilgrim's Progress: now Mr. Greatheart was a strong man. Dinah, Eustace, Isabel, and Scott move through a story of wandering, searching, magic, and escape, from the Wanderer and the Looker-On to the House of Bondage, Olympus, and the Mountain Crest.

Isabel, escaped from those who would keep her back, insists on meeting him at dawn on the mountain-top, at the peaks of Paradise, though darkness falls. Scott enters quietly, reads the scene at a glance, and speaks to Isabel alone in the twilight. Dell mixes romance, desert friendship, and a vision of Greatheart into a tale of loyalty tested by captivity and flight.
13763-the-lamp-in-the-desert:
Ethel M. Dell published this romance in 1919, set partly in the North African desert. Stella, a young Englishwoman, faces a harsh marriage and a lonely outpost life. Major Monck, a stern soldier with a guarded past, becomes her unlikely protector. Desert heat, distance, and gossip press hard on both of them.

Dell builds the story from strong feeling, sacrifice, and slow trust. Stella must choose between duty, pride, and love. Monck must face old guilt before he can offer her a future. The lamp of the title marks guidance through dark places, literal and moral. Dell's fans will recognise her mix of passion and melodrama. The novel moves briskly despite its long length.
1474-the-illustrious-gaudissart:
Balzac's short novel celebrates, and gently mocks, the commercial traveller, a new figure of modern France. Gaudissart, a prince of salesmen, arrives in a provincial town with samples, patter, and boundless confidence, ready to sell anything to anyone, from hats to newspapers to grand ideas.

His campaign among local worthies brings triumphs, blunders, and a famous bargain struck on the strength of talk alone. Balzac enjoys the man's energy even as he exposes the puff behind it. The tale is a lively comedy of commerce, persuasion, and the new age of advertising.
15279-a-letter-addressed-to-the-abbe-ray:
Thomas Paine, secretary for foreign affairs to Congress during the American war, wrote this letter to Abbé Raynal on North American affairs, printed in London in 1792. Raynal's French account of the American Revolution, reprinted in Philadelphia, mistook facts and causes from a distance, Paine argues. His letter corrects them.

Paine, author of Common Sense and Rights of Man, writes with his usual clarity and fire, guarding history from accidental error. The tract shows a founder defending the Revolution's record. Students of Paine and the Revolution will find the letter short, sharp, and historically valuable.
1555-a-passion-in-the-desert:
Balzac's Passion in the Desert opens at a menagerie, where a lady shudders at a tamer working with his hyena, and a companion tells how such a bond can form. In Egypt during the French campaign, a soldier lost in the desert finds shelter with a panther, and man and beast share food, sleep, and a strange, tender companionship.

The tale is short and haunting, and its ending turns the idyll to tragedy. Balzac treats the panther as both animal and mirror of human passion. It is one of his most famous short stories, and a striking fable of love across the divide of species.
16089-england-s-effort:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's England's Effort gathers her letters to an American friend on Britain at war, published by Scribner in 1918 with a preface by Joseph H. Choate. This file is volume two, subtitled The War on All Fronts, with pictures including snow on a British battleship in a North Sea spring. Ward wrote in four strenuous months, with every facility granted by the British government.

Her letters answer American friends whose sympathy lay with the Allies, describing effort, sacrifice, and resolve across the fronts. The prose is earnest, patriotic, and personal, a famous novelist reporting a nation at war. Modern readers gain a contemporary British view of the First World War, written to persuade and to inform.
16178-essays-on-art:
A. Clutton-Brock's Essays on Art, first published by Methuen in London in 1919, gathers criticism on painting, music, and the artist's place. Contents include The Adoration of the Magi, Leonardo da Vinci, The Pompadour in Art, An Unpopular Master, A Defence of Criticism, and The Artist and His Audience. Wilfulness and wisdom, The Magic Flute, process or person, the artist and the tradesman, and professionalism follow.

The opening essay weighs nature's beauty against art's, testing Croce's theory that nature gives only raw material and perception begins the artistic act. Clutton-Brock writes with a critic's clarity and a philosopher's patience. Readers interested in art, taste, and making will find thoughtful, readable essays.
1670-luther-s-little-instruction-book-th:
Short questions and short answers: that is the whole method of Luther's Small Catechism, made so parents could teach children and pastors could teach new members. The Ten Commandments come first, each followed by the question 'What does this mean. ' and a brief, plain explanation.

The Apostles' Creed, the Lord's Prayer, baptism, confession, and the Lord's Supper follow in the same form, made to be learned by heart in the home. The book's aim is practical: parents teaching children, pastors teaching new members, and ordinary believers given words they could hold onto. It remains one of the most widely used summaries of Reformation faith.
16777-the-heart-of-the-desert-kut-le-of-:
Honore Willsie wrote this 1913 desert tale, issued by A. L. Burt in New York with a color frontispiece of a pair riding off into a desert sunset. Chapters move from the Pecos valley, through Indian and white ways, a pursuit, a desert kindergarten, first lessons, a broadening horizon, a long trail, an escape, and a forgotten city. Kut-Le of the desert stands at its heart.

Willsie sets white and native ways side by side in a harsh, beautiful land, with lessons learned by living, not by preaching. The desert itself teaches patience, courage, and sight. Readers who like western tales with a moral core will find a thoughtful, vivid novel of trails, escapes, and a heart changed by the desert.
16917-art:
Clive Bell wrote this 1913 book on art, issued by Frederick A. Stokes in New York and printed in Great Britain. Contents ask what art is. They take up the aesthetic hypothesis and post-impressionism. The metaphysical hypothesis, art and religion, and art and history follow. Art and ethics, the Christian slope, and the classical renaissance appear too. The debt to Cezanne closes the set. A Wei figure of the fifth century fronts the book.

Bell argues that true art stirs a special aesthetic emotion through significant form, not through story or moral. His case for post-impressionism shook English taste. The book remains a landmark of modern art theory, short, bold, and best read by anyone who wants to know why modern art broke with old rules.
17041-the-man-in-court:
Frederic DeWitt Wells, a judge of New York's Municipal Court, wrote this 1917 guide to court life from the bench. Chapters move from night court and civil court to the judge, the anxious jury, the strenuous lawyer, the worried client, and the confused witness. Picking a jury, opening a case, and facing technical objections each get a plain, lively chapter.

Wells writes for lay readers as well as lawyers, with humor and a firm sense of fair play. His night court scenes are sad and vivid, showing law at its most human. Anyone curious about how a trial really feels, beyond the drama of fiction, will find this a clear and humane introduction.
1734-the-secret-places-of-the-heart:
A successful man named Sir Richmond Hardy finds his nerves failing, and a doctor sends him on a motor tour that becomes a confession in motion. A doctor's consultation, a departure from London, and stops at Maidenhead and Stonehenge give the journey its stations. Lady Hardy and other companions force Hardy to face what his work has cost him.

Wells uses the trip as a frame for talk about marriage, women, and the state of England after the war. The book is less a plot than a confession in motion, and its interest lies in Hardy's blunt self-examination, which never quite turns into reform. It shows Wells the novelist of ideas at his most personal.
17373-the-madonna-in-art:
Estelle M. Hurll's Madonna in Art, copyright 1897, studies Mary in painting through eight types: portrait, enthroned, in the sky, pastoral, at home, of love, in adoration, and as witness. Giorgione's Madonna of Castelfranco fronts the book, with Bellini, Perugino, Raphael, Leonardo, Fra Angelico, and Bouguereau among its pictures. A Coleridge motto opens the text: a mother is a mother still, the holiest thing alive.

Hurll writes in plain, devout art prose for general readers, with a bibliography for study. Her chapters help viewers read pose, setting, and symbol in each Madonna. Art lovers will find a warm, classic guide to how painters across centuries pictured motherhood and grace.
17690-the-master-of-appleby-a-novel-tale:
Francis Lynde wrote this novel, published in New York in 1902 by Grosset and Dunlap, with pictures by T. de Thulstrup. Its subtitle promises a tale of the great struggle in the two Carolinas, but chiefly of two gentlemen who loved one and the same lady. Chapters open with whetting a father's sword and knitting up broken ends.

An enemy scores first, a matter may be passed over lightly, and a lost thing never gained follows. Red wrath may heal a wound, a lady has no part, and mercy is tasted, with a golden key unlocking a door ahead. Readers get a Revolutionary romance of the Carolinas, gallant and sentimental. The book suits readers of Lynde and of historical romance.
17753-on-the-antiquity-of-the-chemical-a:
James Mactear delivered this address on the antiquity of the chemical art. He was a fellow of the Chemical Society and of the Chemical Institute, and the address opened the chemical section of a scientific meeting. Mactear, a member of the international jury at Paris in 1878 and a medallist of the Society of Arts, speaks as a senior figure of Victorian chemical industry.

Readers get a survey of chemistry's ancient roots, from early arts and crafts to the science of Mactear's day. The address suits readers of the history of chemistry and of Victorian scientific oratory. Its pride in an old art marks its period.
18362-fifteen-thousand-useful-phrases-a-:
Grenville Kleiser compiled this handbook of felicitous expressions for enriching the vocabulary, sold in cloth at a dollar and sixty cents. Kleiser, known for books on speaking in public and building mental power, aimed the volume at writers and speakers who wanted fresh, exact phrases at hand. The book holds fifteen thousand phrases, grouped for use rather than for reading straight through.

Its pages offer short turns for judgment, praise, blame, and feeling, such as phrases on private interests, on consulting authority before judging, and on flattery. A transcriber's note adds plain definitions of unfamiliar words in brackets. Readers get a working tool: a store of ready phrases to lift dull writing into clear, lively English without hunting through a dictionary.
19063-little-alice-s-palace-or-the-sunny:
Published in London in 1872, this short moral tale for children centres on Little Alice, who lives in a small brown cottage by a country road. She has a sunny temper and talks to grass, flowers, and birds as if they were friends. The tale links her good cheer to the state of her home.

A kind lady visits a ragged child in a dirty cottage and shows her how to clean, wash, and set the place in order. Sunlight, fresh air, and tidy rooms follow, and the child learns a new way of living. Young readers get a plain lesson: a cheerful heart shows itself in care for home and for others.
19166-the-quirt:
B. M. Bower wrote this 1920 western novel about the Quirt ranch and its mighty neighbour, the Sawtooth. Senator Warfield, a modern range man, backs every scheme for progress, while the small Quirt folk live hemmed in by Sawtooth land, fences, and scarce water at Quirt Creek. Small fish, the narrator says, live uneasily among big fish.

Lorraine Hunter, who calls herself a Western girl, enters the feud, and Al's gun speaks in the front piece scene. Land, water, and pride drive the quarrel. Readers get a lively ranch tale of power, pluck, and the fight of a small outfit to hold its ground.
1943-louis-lambert:
At Montoire, a little town in the Vendômois, a boy named Louis Lambert grows up with a mind too large for his life. His father owned a tannery of no great size in the town. His ideas about thought and will, and about the unseen beings before whom people tremble, mark him early as both genius and madman.

The novel follows Lambert through school, where his ideas about thought, will, and the supernatural beings before whom people tremble. Personifications of feelings and magnified desires — mark him as a genius and as a madman. Balzac writes the story as a portrait of a mind too large for its life, and it remains one of his most personal books.
19554-dick-lionheart:
Mary Rowles Jarvis wrote this children's tale of Dick Lionheart, published in London with four pictures. Dick, a boy with something to love, fights a fire, dashes for freedom, rides in a carrier's wagon, and loses and finds his dog Pat, who rushes to his feet in joy.

Later chapters bring a brave stand against a horse, a stopped burglary, and success at last. The book's short, stirring chapters made it a favorite for young readers who liked pluck, animals, and a hero who never thinks of danger before helping.
19696-the-joyful-heart:
Robert Haven Schauffler wrote this book in defense of joy, published in Boston and New York in the mid nineteen teens. Chapters cover enthusiasm, the brimming cup, the auto-comrade, printed joy, and the joyful heart for poets, with a nod to mechanical music.

Schauffler argues that nobly happy people form the power and beauty of the state, quoting Jean Finot on the science of happiness. The book is a cheerful counter to gloom, urging readers to find joy in sport, art, and daily life. A chapter of enthusiasms and a closing note on masters by proxy round out the defense.
19818-dixie-hart:
Dixie Hart, dated 1910, is a romance of the Southern mountains. Its opening sweeps a veranda floor in plain mountain country. An old man and old woman sit in chairs propped against the weatherboarding. Their dress is the plainest of mountain attire. A young woman does the sweeping, disguised by few attempts at adornment. The scene sets class and region in one glance.

Mountain romances sold the Cumberlands and Smokies to city readers. Dialect, feuds, and courtship under hardship were the stock elements. Dixie Hart's title names its heroine as a regional emblem. Such novels preserved folk speech while romancing it. They also fixed stereotypes that later writers fought. This one is a fair specimen of the shelf.
20155-the-white-desert:
Courtney Ryley Cooper published The White Desert in 1922, a novel of snow country and crime. Melt-water from the hills feeds the streams in spring thaw. A jaybird calls harshly above a robin nesting in green aspen. That clash of harsh and sweet notes opens the book's world.

The white desert is snow land, empty, bright, and deadly cold. Cooper sets law men, outlaws, and love amid drifts and pines. His westerns often turned on the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Readers get a northern tale where weather itself acts as a foe.
20789-the-grammar-school-boys-snowbound-:
Young Dutcher puffs out his chest on the ice, keen to look like a big man. His schoolmates in Dick and Co. at Winter Sports refuse to rate him so high. H. Irving Hancock sets the scene with a grin at small vanity.

Dick Prescott and his chums fill Hancock's Grammar School Boys set of tales. Snow, skating, and winter scrapes drive this snowbound volume. Hancock wrote shelves of boys' books on school, sport, and army life. His tales prize pluck, fairness, and clean fun. Readers get a brisk slice of American boyhood as it was sold to young readers a century ago.
21255-the-eagle-s-heart:
Hamlin Garland's 1900 Western novel follows Mose, called the young eagle. It traces him from youth through love affairs to a trial and a spell in a cage, meaning prison. Chapter titles track his rises and falls: the eagle strikes, his eyes grow dim, the cage opens, and he mounts again. Round-ups on the Cannon Ball range frame his working life.

Later parts take Mose back to Wagon Wheel, set him guarding sheep, and send him into strange lands before the circle completes. Garland knew the plains and cow country well. The eagle image carries a restless cowboy's life between wild freedom and settling down.
21421-the-magnificent-montez-from-courte:
Horace Wyndham tells the wild life of Lola Montez in The Magnificent Montez, from courtesan to convert. Montez, Countess of Landsfeld, died in 1861 after a career that few could match. Dancer, lover of kings, and lecturer, she crossed three continents in high style.

The chapters run from a hasty marriage and court fights to the Bavarian king Ludwig's court. There she rose as the king's mistress before a storm brought her down. Later chapters follow her to America and Australia, then to a quiet end. Aldous Huxley's tart line on her fame opens this brisk, full life.
21633-the-man-of-the-desert:
Grace Livingston Hill sets The Man of the Desert in Arizona, in a tale copyrighted in 1914. A silent private rail car, its curtains parted, draws a crowd at a little station. Seven Indigenous onlookers and women from nearby shacks watch the strange car.

Chapters named Prospecting, The Man, and The Desert open the tale. A quest, a trail, and a camp follow, then revelation and renunciation. Hill, who wrote Marcia Schuyler and Dawn of the Morning, mixes romance with faith. Her hero's call to service in the desert gives the love story its backbone and its end.
2176-seven-discourses-on-art:
Sir Joshua Reynolds, founder president of the Royal Academy, gave seven discourses on art at the opening of its schools and at prize-giving meetings. The discourses lay down principles for young painters. Reynolds gave the discourses between 1769 and 1790, as president of the Academy.

Reynolds urges study of the great masters, ideal beauty, and the general truths of art over mere copying. His clear good sense made the discourses a classic of art theory, read by painters and writers alike. His ideal beauty, drawn from Raphael and Michelangelo, guided British painters for a century.
22390-prince-or-chauffeur-a-story-of-new:
Prince or Chauffeur? is a story of Newport, the rich resort town. Its opening puts a traveler in a train's sleeping berth. His bag sits stowed under a lower berth as he hesitates.

A half-hour must pass before the train starts. He is not sleepy, having dozed most of the way from Washington. Threshing about in the hot berth holds no appeal. That frowning indecision starts a tale of hidden identity. The title asks whether a stranger is royalty or a servant. Newport society, with its parties and fortunes, supplies the stage. Readers get light romance among America's summer rich.
22398-the-heiress-of-wyvern-court:
E. Searchfield wrote The Heiress of Wyvern Court, a novel named for its heroine's home. The preserved scene opens in a railway carriage. A traveler settles in with cricket bat and fishing rod.

A knowing-looking little hamper sits on the seat beside him. Then away goes the snorting steam horse, train and all. Out comes an abrupt question that starts the talk. Such openings promise country-house society and young people's sport. An heiress, by the title, stands to inherit Wyvern Court. Readers get a period novel of trains, estates, and manners. Its charm lies in small props and quick dialogue.
22587-northern-nut-growers-association-t:
The Thirty-fourth Annual Report of the Northern Nut Growers Association is the yearly record of a society devoted to growing nut trees in northern climates. The catalog record names no editor and gives no year. The association gathered growers, scientists, and hobbyists who tested which nut varieties could thrive in cold regions.

The surviving sample lists members and contacts state by state and province by province, from Alberta and British Columbia to Georgia and Quebec. That roll shows a wide, organized network sharing stock and results across North America. Annual reports like this one carried meeting papers, variety trials, and planting advice. Orchardists and historians of American farming can still mine it for what growers knew and tried.
22597-question-of-comfort:
Question of Comfort is a story set inside the world of Disneyland's public relations office in Burbank. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its narrator recalls starting, as most newcomers did, with low-pay, low-level jobs, and not minding much, since a foot in the right door was prize enough.

Within six months the narrator had climbed far enough to pitch an idea of their own. That quick rise through the happiest bureaucracy on earth sets up the tale's questions about work, comfort, and ambition. The setting gives the story a rare behind-the-scenes flavor from the early Disney machine. It should please readers curious about show-business offices and the price of a comfortable chair.
2282-tales-for-fifteen-or-imagination-an:
James Fenimore Cooper, writing for his own daughters, offers moral tales meant to train imagination and heart in equal measure. Tales for Fifteen pairs stories of youthful error and correction, with heroines and heroes learning prudence, kindness, and self-command. The tone is earnest and instructive, as befits a father's book.

The tales show Cooper outside his frontier epics, working in the domestic and didactic mode of his time. Modern readers may find the morals old-fashioned, but the stories reveal the values of an early American household. The collection interests students of Cooper and of children's literature alike.
23663-tom-slade-on-a-transport:
Percy K. Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade Boy Scout books, published this wartime volume in 1918 with the approval of the Boy Scouts of America. Tom, now bound for service, ships out on a transport, and the voyage tests the scout virtues of loyalty, courage, and good turns under real wartime strain.

Chapters follow Tom through a good turn and a discovery, a strange light, and a dark hold below decks. Later come an arrest and a spell in the guardhouse, and a moment when he does most of the talking and takes all the blame. Friends old and new, including Frenchy, share the voyage, and the book gives young readers a scout's-eye view of going to war by sea.
24191-life-immovable-first-part:
Kostes Palamas wrote these poems, translated by Aristides E. Phoutrides with an introduction and notes by the translator, and published by Harvard University Press in 1919. The volume is called Life Immovable, First Part, and its contents present Palamas as a new world-poet. Poems include Fatherlands in twelve parts, a set of sonnets, Epiphany, Makaria, The Market Place, and Loves.

Later pieces range from When Polylas Died and Soldier and Maker to the Athena relief, the Huntress relief, a father's song, Imagination, Makaria's death, and an Orphic hymn. The translator's notes guide English readers through a Greek poet of wide scope. Readers get a substantial first part of a major modern Greek voice, in careful translation.
24347-emmy-lou-her-book-and-heart:
George Madden Martin wrote this book of school stories, published by Grosset and Dunlap in New York, reaching a fifteenth impression, with pictures by Charles Louis Hinton. Its motto, from the New England Primer, runs my book and heart must never part. The book is dedicated to the author's sister, the Aunt Cordelia of these stories. Emmy Lou, copying digits in school, looks up to find a boy in the next row making signs to her.

He is a square little boy, freckled across the nose, with a broad, constant smile. His knowledge of the Primer World seems limitless to Emmy Lou, who knows none of the seventy other children around her. Stories include The Right Promethean Fire, A Little Feminine Casabianca, Hare-and-Tortoise, The Play's the Thing, and Venus or Minerva. Readers get a tender schoolroom book of a small girl's heart.
24705-the-woman-with-a-stone-heart:
O. W. Coursey, a United States volunteer, wrote this romance of the Philippine War, published at Mitchell, South Dakota, in 1914 by the Educator Supply Company. Coursey, author of a history and geography of the Philippine Islands, dedicated the book to his wife. She bade him farewell as a bride of eighteen months when his train of soldier boys left for war.

His heroine, the woman with a stone heart, faces love, war, and loss in the Philippines. Coursey's romance mixes soldiering with sentiment, from a man who served there. Readers get a period romance of the Philippine campaign, earnest, patriotic, and very much of its time.
24828-margaret-montfort:
Laura E. Richards wrote Margaret Montfort as one of her New England village tales, praised for its delicate touch on country life. Margaret, a young girl, comes under her uncle's care, and the story follows her through a house full of quiet tension. A night scene finds her led down a felt-carpeted passage to her uncle's study, where a rustle of silk and a flash of light bring a sudden shock.

Richards keeps the tone gentle even as secrets stir: family duty, hidden feelings, and a girl learning to read the adults around her. The book suits readers who enjoy quiet, old-fashioned stories where character, not action, carries the plot.
25268-child-life-in-art:
Estelle M. Hurll's Child-Life in Art, published in Boston in 1895, studies how artists have pictured childhood. Its frontispiece is Raphael's Sistine Madonna, and its motto from Lowell calls children God's apostles, sent to preach love, hope, and peace.

Hurll argues that the Christ-child set the highest ideal for child pictures, shaping all later images of innocence. Later chapters turn to cottage scenes from the Hessian, Bavarian, and Swiss Alps, where flaxen-haired children play in rooms with fiddle-back chairs and diamond-paned windows. The book is a gentle guide to looking at art through children.
25686-the-iraq-study-group-report:
James A. Baker III and Lee H. Hamilton co-chair the Iraq Study Group Report, joined by members including Lawrence Eagleburger, Vernon Jordan, Edwin Meese, Sandra Day O'Connor, Leon Panetta, William Perry, Charles Robb, and Alan Simpson. A letter from the co-chairs and an executive summary open the report.

Part one assesses Iraq's security, politics, economics, and international support, weighs consequences of continued decline, and tests alternatives such as precipitate withdrawal, staying the course, more troops, and devolution to three regions. Part two sets a new approach, outward through diplomacy and inward by helping Iraqis help themselves.
26149-left-guard-gilbert:
Ralph Henry Barbour's 1916 school story follows the boys of Brimfield, a boarding school with a keen football team, through a full season of practice, games, and scrapes. Don, a boy from Kansas, arrives to find coach Robey, rivals, and friends such as Tim and Amy. Chapter titles promise fire-fighting, jokes on masters, and a search for adventure between matches.

The plot turns on setbacks on and off the field. Don faces a spell dropped from the team, a doctor's visit, and a cross-examination. The final chapters then build to the big game and the title role of left guard. It is a warm, old-style tale of school loyalty, pluck, and team spirit, written for young readers of its day.
26324-ravensdene-court:
J. S. Fletcher's Ravensdene Court, issued by Alfred A. Knopf in July 1922, is a mystery told by an expert in old books and documents. The narrator leaves London for Ravensdene Court on March 8, 1912, after a February letter asks him to inspect, value, and judge an ancient library. The house stands on a remote stretch of the Northumbrian coast, near Alnwick, far from his usual haunts.

Chapters promise an inn on the cliff, a tobacco box, secret theft, Yellowface, an enlarged photograph, and the spoils of sacrilege. Later come a ship broker, a Chinese gentleman, a fourth Chinaman, and a silk cap. A detective named Scarterfield hunts a man called Chuh Fen, linked to an Elizabeth Robinson affair. The book blends library lore with coastal danger.
26420-the-convert:
Elizabeth Robins's 1907 novel, published in 1913 in this edition, follows a young woman drawn into the campaign for women's votes. The heroine first appears arriving for dinner at the Tunbridge house, sent upstairs past the drawing-room to the night nursery, where children greet her with shrieks of joy. Society, nursery, and drawing-room give way, chapter by chapter, to committee rooms and deputations.

The novel's argument peaks in a roll call of the unrepresented. Textile workers, women who waited on the Prime Minister, and half a million trade union members appear, and above all unorganized women whose voices are never heard in public. Compelling women to work over hours is illegal, Robins insists, yet no one sees the laws fairly applied for those without votes. The heroine's conversion becomes the book's spine.
26550-children-of-the-desert:
Louis Dodge published this border novel with Charles Scribner's Sons in 1917, dedicating it to friends of Eagle Pass and Piedras Negras in the good old days. It opens with a September wedding in the late eighties, in the little Episcopal church at Eagle Pass, Texas, where Harboro weds Sylvia Little before a large and curious audience. Desert, sage, cactus, and the Rio Grande frame the town.

Later parts carry titles such as The Time of Flame, Fectnor the People's Advocate, The Horse with the Golden Dapples, and A Wind from the North. Border elections, with corrals built to capture Mexican voters, show the rough politics of Maverick County. Harboro and Sylvia, both extraordinary in their way, anchor a tale of love and power on the frontier.
26836-cases-of-organic-diseases-of-the-h:
John C. Warren read this paper before the counsellors of the Massachusetts Medical Society and printed it in Boston in 1809. Its case histories pair bedside symptoms with dissections made hours after death, so that each patient's complaints can be checked against the state of the heart itself. Two plates open the volume, showing thickened aortic valves, bony growths across a valve, and fleshy thickening of the aorta.

Warren wrote because heart disease was often mistaken for asthma, consumption, or water in the chest. Taken one by one, the signs look alike, he argues, but their pattern and degree differ. The cases aim to pick out signs that belong to the heart alone, so physicians can tell organic disease apart from its look-alikes.
27194-the-enjoyment-of-art:
Carleton Noyes's The Enjoyment of Art, published by Houghton, Mifflin in 1903 and dedicated to Robert Henri and Van D. Perrine, asks why crowds fill public galleries. Noyes notes that visitors come from every station and walk of life, proof that pictures appeal to no one class alone.

The book moves from the picture and the man to the artist, arguing that character grows from heredity, environment, training, and the inexplicable ego. A chapter on Madame Bovary as a triumph of realism shows Noyes testing literary method against the same questions of seeing and feeling.
27524-hampton-court:
Walter Jerrold described this Hampton Court, pictured by E. W. Haslehust, in Blackie's Beautiful England series, published in London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1912. Companion volumes in the series include Dickens-Land, Winchester, the Isle of Wight, and the New Forest.

Illustrations show the Lion Gate, the great gatehouse, a corner of Wolsey's kitchen, and Anne Boleyn's gateway in Clock Court. Fountain Court, the great hall, the pond garden, and the long water in winter follow. Jerrold quotes Pope on the structure of majestic frame by the Thames. For combined beauty and historical interest near London, he says, no place surpasses it.
27646-the-orchestral-conductor-theory-of:
Hector Berlioz wrote this theory of the orchestral conductor's art, published by Carl Fischer in New York in 1902. Berlioz calls music the most exacting of all the arts, and its full interpretation among the rarest achievements.

The composer, he says, is almost the only creative artist dependent on a multitude of intermediate agents between himself and the public. Those agents, intelligent or stupid, devoted or hostile, can add brilliancy to his work or disfigure and destroy it. Singers are often accused of being the most dangerous of them, but Berlioz disagrees. The most formidable, in his judgment, is the conductor of the orchestra.
27997-robert-orange-being-a-continuation:
John Oliver Hobbes published Robert Orange in London with T. Fisher Unwin in 1900, a continuation of the history of Robert Orange, M.P., and a sequel to The School for Saints. The novel opens in October 1869, with a small yellow brougham before the Earl of Garrow's town residence in St. James's Square.

Lady Sara-Louise-Tatiana-Valérie De Treverell, only child of the ninth earl and mistress of his house since her mother's death, steps out in mauve silk and orders the carriage to the Carlton Club. Hobbes's society novel follows politics, romance, and Catholic feeling in late Victorian London.
2901-studies-and-essays-censorship-and-a:
John Galsworthy's essays on censorship and art argue against the British censorship of plays, then the only official censorship in a country of free institutions. Galsworthy notes that most of his countrymen treat that censorship as a bulwark for their comfort against the spiritual researches of bolder spirits. He asks whether a principle so grateful to the majority should be extended to every institution, and answers with irony.

The art essays turn inward, describing how a work steals the viewer out of himself for a moment, linking him to something universal by making him forget the individual in him. Color and form, not practical thought, do the work. The essays remain a clear statement of Galsworthy's belief that art needs freedom to do its quiet job.
29201-comments-on-the-taxonomy-and-geogr:
E. Raymond Hall and E. Lendell Cockrum published this scientific paper in 1952, in the University of Kansas Publications of the Museum of Natural History, volume 5, number 23. It comments on the taxonomy and geographic distribution of North American microtines, the group of small rodents that includes voles and lemmings.

The authors prepared maps of where these animals live and found conflicting statements in the literature, along with identifications that, if accepted, would distort the ranges. They sort out which names and ranges hold up. Readers get a specialist paper, dense with tables, that shows how museum scientists clean up the record of where species actually occur.
297-the-flirt:
Valentine Corliss walks up Corliss Street on the hottest August afternoon in a white serge suit. Booth Tarkington's Flirt opens in Capitol City, a provincial town that fancies itself cosmopolitan. Corliss Street is its Park Lane and Fifth Avenue at once.

Tarkington follows a flirt's charm, vanity, and damage through drawing rooms and summer resorts. The novel's social comedy bites at ambition, marriage markets, and self-deception. Its heroine's name became shorthand for a type. The book shows Tarkington's Midwestern eye at work. Tarkington's novels of Midwestern manners won him lasting fame.
30188-the-fifth-queen-and-how-she-came-t:
Ford Madox Ford opens his Fifth Queen trilogy with the coming of a new queen to the Tudor court, in three parts: The Coming, The House of Eyes, and The King Moves. The first scene finds Magister Nicholas Udal, pedagogue to the Lady Mary, hungry and cold in a muddy lane at Austin Friars. He curses the porter of the great house of the Lord Privy Seal. Bare orchards, dry hedges, and gilded vanes set a wintry, watchful mood.

Udal, a man to whom Latin comes more readily than common speech, stands at the edge of a maze of small cottages built from old friars' stables and offices. Ford writes the court world through such small, vivid figures, letting power show in houses, gates, and cold lanes before it shows in council. Readers who like rich period detail will find the opening a strong door into the trilogy.
30436-hope-mills-or-between-friend-and-s:
Amanda M. Douglas sets this novel at Hope Mills, where ties of friendship shade into courtship and the choice between a friend and a sweetheart shapes the story. Published in Boston in 1879, it belongs to her long run of domestic novels for family readers, several of which are listed alongside it in the front matter.

Douglas builds the plot from household life, work, loyalty, and affection, letting small decisions carry moral weight. Characters weigh duty against desire and learn how promises made in friendship can complicate love. The tone stays warm and plain, with an eye for home, mill-town routine, and the steady claims of kin and neighbors.
30472-needlework-as-art:
Lady M. Alford writes Needlework as Art, published in London in 1886 and dedicated by permission to the Queen. Alford thanks the Queen for graciously accepting the dedication, saying it casts light on a subject worthy of attention, even as she doubts her ability to do it justice.

She hopes to supply a missing piece in the art writing of her day, laying her work at the Queen's feet with loyal devotion. An illustration shows Telemachus and Penelope, linking needlework to classical story. Alford treats embroidery as fine art, not mere craft, arguing for its design, color, and place in a cultured home.
30636-the-somnambulist-and-the-detective:
Allan Pinkerton's great detective stories include The Somnambulist and Detectives as number seven in a long series, alongside The Mollie Maguires and Detectives, Strikers, Communists, and Detectives, and Criminal Reminiscences and Detectives. Other volumes cover the model town, spiritualists, expressmen, Claude Melnotte, Mississippi outlaws, and gypsies.

Later titles add Bucholz, the railroad forger, bank robbers, the burglar's fate, a double life, professional thieves, and thirty years a detective. Pinkerton's series presents cases from his agency's files, blending true crime with detective craft. The somnambulist volume turns on sleepwalking, mystery, and detection in the classic Pinkerton mode. The tales are short and brisk. They move from case to case, with clues, chases, and plain talk, so a reader can follow each job from start to end.
30649-last-resort:
Stephen Bartholomew writes Last Resort, a science fiction story from Analog, April 1963, illustrated by George Schelling. Its opening note treats hysterical strength at the physical level as well known, then wonders what the same phenomenon at the psychological level might do.

The narrator inflates a rubber balloon and sets it adrift, hoping that in free fall it will drift slowly toward a leak. That act follows discovery of trouble, after long thought about the distance from Pacific Grove, California, to Mars. He fears he will never breathe eucalyptus odor again. Bartholomew turns isolation and mental strain into a tense space tale.
30671-the-brownings-their-life-and-art:
Lilian Whiting wrote this 1911 life of Robert Browning and Elizabeth Barrett Browning, two poets whose marriage became one of the best known love stories in English letters. Whiting draws on letters, friends, and her own visits, and she dedicates the book to their son, Robert Barrett Browning, painter and sculptor. The front pages quote Elizabeth Barrett Browning on poetry as its own great reward.

Chapters trace Robert's youth and early poems, Elizabeth's childhood at Hope End, their courtship and flight to Italy, and their later years as writers and parents. Whiting treats their work and their home life as one story, with music, books, and faith shaping both poets. Readers new to the Brownings get a warm, detailed guide to their lives, while fans will enjoy the letters and small scenes Whiting gathered.
30686-little-tales-of-the-desert:
Ethel Twycross Foster writes Little Tales of the Desert, illustrated by Hernando G. Villa and published by the author in Los Angeles, copyrighted in 1913. Foster, a member of the Suffolk Bar, opens with Christmas on the Desert, Trade Rats, and A Chat with Mrs. Cottontail.

Later tales add Rabbits and Cactus Burrs, The Dangerous Pet, A Visit to Palm Springs, and The Road-Runner. A Strange Capture and A Desert May Party close the list. Christmas on the Desert opens with Mary worried, since tomorrow will be Christmas, a day she always passed near New York City. Foster blends desert nature with gentle, child-friendly stories.
30885-heart:
Henry Slesar wrote this short story, printed in Amazing Stories in January 1957, about a man who is used to buying his way out of trouble. Fletcher Monk lives by three questions: where can he find a thing, how much will it cost, and when can it be delivered? Now doctors tell him that what he needs is not for sale, and Monk answers with a snort and a challenge. The story's title points to the organ at stake, and to the bargain Monk cannot make.

A Cardiophone listens, hums, and records, tracing peaks and precipices on white paper as it tracks systole and diastole. Rostov begs Monk to relax, while Monk protests that he is relaxed, and demands his shirt and his freedom from the wires. Slesar turns a heart exam into a tense, ironic tale about wealth, control, and a body that will not obey a price.
30973-east-of-the-sun-and-west-of-the-mo:
Held here is a book of old tales from the North, illustrated by Kay Nielsen and published by George H. Doran in New York. Its contents run from East of the Sun and West of the Moon and The Blue Belt. Prince Lindworm, The Lassie and Her Godmother, and The Husband Who Was to Mind the House follow. They continue with The Lad Who Went to the North Wind and The Three Princesses of Whiteland.

Later tales include Soria Moria Castle, The Giant Who Had No Heart in His Body, The Princess on the Glass Hill, The Widow's Son, and The Three Billy Goats Gruff. They close with The Cat on the Dovrefell and One's Own Children Are Always Prettiest. Nielsen's pictures, including a bear telling a girl to hold tight by his shaggy coat, give the book its magic. It is a classic collection of Norwegian folk tales.
31215-a-world-apart:
Sam Merwin Jr.'s science fiction story follows Coulter, a prosperous middle-aged man driving back to a hometown unvisited in twenty years after a long lunch with cocktails. A small bump jolts him from reverie. Suddenly the road has changed: the graded ten-car highway is now a narrow tar thoroughfare, high-crowned, with blind crossings, pine woods, and antique houses that look disturbingly familiar.

Most men, the story's introduction notes, would welcome a chance to live their lives a second time, but Coulter did not. What follows is a time-slip tale of return and regret, asking whether a second pass at life would mend anything at all.
31540-marguerite-de-roberval-a-romance-o:
T. G. Marquis's Marguerite de Roberval, a romance of the days of Jacques Cartier, was published in Toronto by the Copp Clark Company in 1899. Its first chapter opens with a narrator who finds narrow, cramped streets a torture, and longs for the ocean above all. Five years penned up have left him desperate to slip across the Atlantic in La Hermine, without leave of king or blessing of priest. Gold and diamonds are there in plenty, and a road to the Indies.

Marguerite herself, the heroine of the title, belongs to the legend of a woman abandoned on an island in the St. Lawrence world of Cartier's voyages. Marquis builds his romance from that legend and from the age of exploration. Readers of Canadian historical fiction will find a spirited tale of the sea, exile, and the New World as Europeans first imagined it.
31556-dick-in-the-desert:
James Otis's Dick in the Desert, in the Sunshine Library series, opens in a beautiful Nevada valley between Fox Peak and Smoke Creek Desert. The Indians named it Buffalo Meadows, for the great bison herds once found there, before white men hunted merely for sport. Travelers halting at the last watercourse before the desert called it Comfort Hollow. A travel-stained party, retracing its steps after a fruitless search for a home among the foothills of the Sierras, halts there on a September afternoon.

Dick, the boy of the title, belongs to that party, and his desert adventures follow. Otis, a prolific writer for boys, builds the story from the western landscape itself: valleys, deserts, and the search for a home. Readers of boys' adventure will find a straightforward, outdoor tale, where a young hero learns the desert's hard lessons.
31620-vashti-or-until-death-us-do-part:
Augusta Evans Wilson's novel Vashti, or Until Death Us Do Part, was published by the A. L. Burt Company of New York, entered in 1869 by George W. Carleton and again in 1897 by Mrs. Augusta J. Evans Wilson. Wilson was already known as the author of Beulah, Macaria, Infelice, St. Elmo, and Inez. Her frontispiece shows a stranger raising his hat to ask a young woman's name, and she answers Salome Owen, while he gives his own as Ulpian Gray.

The novel follows Salome and Ulpian through a long story of love, grief, and resolve, in the high romantic manner of Wilson's best-known books. Vashti is a substantial nineteenth-century novel, and it shows Wilson's gift for heroines who endure.
32131-the-kenzie-report:
Mark Clifton's story, printed in If in May 1953, centres on Kenzie MacKenzie, a man his lab mates call mad about ants. Its tagline gives the moral: leave well enough alone, and look what happened to Kenzie, who did not. The narrator works in the same lab. Kenzie ambles down the street, with sandy, uncombed hair and a vague, unfocused gaze. He looks as if dreaming of his girl, while in fact thinking of ants.

The lab fellows put up with Kenzie through fondness and a little pride. He can pull them out of a technical hole. He gives them a safe topic when security bars other talk. The department chief knows it too. Kenzie has solved a few knotty problems. Readers get a lab comedy with a sting: a brilliant, ant-obsessed scientist whose hobby may outgrow its jar.
32454-calvert-and-penn-or-the-growth-of-:
Brantz Mayer's discourse Calvert and Penn, delivered in Philadelphia before the Pennsylvania Historical Society on April 8, 1852, traces civil and religious liberty in America through the planting of Maryland and Pennsylvania. Mayer opens with a Chinese rite: families keep a hall of ancestors and, once a year, leave ordinary toil to honour forebears at their tombs with festivity and worship. That wholesome exercise of memory, he argues, teaches neither blame nor flattery, but respect.

From that image, Mayer turns to George Calvert and William Penn, whose colonies tested tolerance, charter rights, and relations with Native peoples and neighbours. The discourse, printed for the society in Baltimore, suits readers interested in colonial foundations, religious freedom, and the ideas that shaped American liberty. Its mid-nineteenth-century voice gives the argument a period flavour.
33179-personal-recollections-of-the-civi:
James Madison Stone's memoir recalls his service as a private in the 21st Volunteer Regiment of Infantry from Massachusetts during the Civil War. Published by the author in 1918, it opens with learning to be a soldier, the move from Camp Lincoln to the front, and early days at Baltimore and Annapolis. Stone writes of picket duty, camp food, escapes aided on the march, and the small scenes that stayed with him long after.

The book is a soldier's own record, not a general's history, and its strength is its close detail of common life in war. Stone dedicates it to his regiment and their descendants, and his tone is warm and plain. Readers who want the war as one man lived it, day by day, will find here a vivid and honest account.
33642-earth-alert:
Kris Neville writes a science fiction novelette, first published in Imagination Stories of Science and Fantasy in February 1953, about mutant powers loose on an unaware Earth. A sidenote asks what defense Earth could raise against mutant science: telepathy, invisibility, teleportation, especially since Earth does not know it is in danger. The story opens with Julia, twenty-four, inheriting money from an obscure California uncle.

After taxes and expenses, the court transfers just over twenty thousand dollars to her bank account. Julia, a small, slender bookstore worker with bright eyes and an infectious smile, gives two weeks' notice and buys new clothes. Her plan, unspoken, is to shop around for a husband. Neville uses that ordinary beginning to launch a strange, suspenseful tale of hidden powers and human desire.
33650-new-west-indian-spiders-bulletin-o:
Nathan Banks describes new West Indian spiders in this short 1914 article from the Bulletin of the American Museum of Natural History, volume thirty-three, article forty-one, pages 639 to 642. The new species came from material collected by F. E. Lutz and Charles W. Leng in Cuba and by Lutz in Puerto Rico, with types held at the American Museum. Banks gives precise descriptions of each form.

The first species treated, from Naguabo, Puerto Rico, is described in minute detail. Pale cephalothorax with a black median mark, pale abdomen with a black median stripe, long legs, and measurements down to millimeters for head, abdomen, and femora. The article is a compact taxonomic record, useful to arachnologists tracing Caribbean spider diversity and the history of museum collecting.
34075-the-new-gresham-encyclopedia-atreb:
This third part of volume one of the New Gresham Encyclopedia, published in London in 1922 by the Gresham Publishing Company, carries the alphabet from Atrebates toward Bedlis. Plates include bacteria, and a map in colour covers Australia. A key to pronunciation opens the part, marking accent by syllable or by a simple transliteration system.

Vowel sounds run from fate and bare through alms, fat, fall, and rural, to machine, met, her, pine, and pin, with French and German examples beside. The part serves readers who want clear speech with their facts. It remains a handy slice of a great home encyclopedia.
3475-the-efficiency-expert:
Edgar Rice Burroughs writes an adventure novel about Jimmy Torrance, a college athlete who must make his way in the business world. The story opens with Jimmy winning the university boxing championship in a bloody fourth round, after four years in which he captained the football team and starred at first base. College glory, however, does not pay rent.

Jimmy takes work as an efficiency expert, a new kind of job in early twentieth century America, and learns that offices have their own fights. Burroughs mixes romance, rivalry, and comic scrapes as Jimmy tries to prove himself. The novel suits readers who enjoy Burroughs beyond Mars and Tarzan, in a brisk tale of youth and work.
3611-second-shetland-truck-system-report:
William Guthrie presents this report on the truck system in Shetland, the practice by which workers were paid in goods or store credit rather than in cash. In Shetland's fishing and farming economy, landlords and merchants often ran the stores where their tenants and crews had to spend their earnings. The system bound workers to their employers and hid the true value of their wages.

Guthrie's second report gathers evidence, testimony, and findings on how the system worked and whom it harmed. It belongs to the long nineteenth century campaign against truck, which Parliament later curbed by law. The report suits readers interested in labor history, Scottish islands, and the slow reform of workers' pay.
3621-peg-o-my-heart:
J Hartley Manners writes the novel of his famous comedy Peg o' My Heart, about an Irish girl named Peg whose plain speech wins over wealthy relatives and suitors. The preface records the play's success. By December 1922 it had been played more than eight thousand times in the United States and Canada. It had also played more than six thousand times in Britain and Ireland, and dozens of times in India and the Orient. A composer, Dr Hugo Felix, was setting an operetta version to music.

Manners writes Peg as a warm, funny heroine who refuses to trade honesty for fashion. The story mixes romance, family pride, and stage comedy. Readers who enjoy light, sentimental theater in novel form will find a cheerful tale that explains why Peg charmed audiences around the world.
3631-on-the-significance-of-science-and-:
Leo Tolstoy writes an essay, drawn from his larger work What to Do, on the meaning of science and art in modern life. He argues that experimental, positive science has become the excuse by which people freed from toil justify their idle lives. The theory claims one indubitable method for studying human societies, yet it leaves the poor to their fate while praising progress.

Tolstoy sets this science against older wisdom, naming Rousseau, Lessing, Spinoza, and Bruno as thinkers who asked what life is for. He asks whether art and science serve the people or merely amuse the rich. The essay suits readers who want Tolstoy's sharpest critique of modern culture in short form.
3773-hopes-and-fears-for-art:
William Morris delivered these five lectures to argue that art must serve all people, not a pampered few. The five lectures take turn making the case, from craft workshops to city streets. Their titles run from The Lesser Arts and The Art of the People to The Beauty of Life, Making the Best of It, and The Prospects of Architecture in Civilization. Morris holds that the murder of art in poor districts has its match in the dullness of rich ones, and that no polished few can rise above the squalor below them.

The lectures plead for honest work, beautiful homes, and streets worth walking, with decoration as daily bread, not luxury. Morris writes as a craftsman and a socialist, plain and earnest. Readers who care about design, labor, or cities will find a short book of large claims, still quoted when beauty and justice are weighed together.
3787-nature-and-art:
Elizabeth Inchbald, once a poor farmer's daughter from Standingfield who stole away to the London stage, wrote this novel of feeling and society. The long introduction follows her own life, from a girlhood love of the Bury Theatre to a hard start in London and marriage to an actor. The novel itself turns on the contrast its title names, between simple nature and polished art, as lived by young people in a world of rank and talk.

Agnes stands at the center of the tale's pathos, a girl whose lover William writes rarely and late, leaving her to face her parents and neighbors with a breaking heart. Inchbald asks whether fine manners hide or heal such wounds. Readers who like eighteenth century novels of sentiment will find a book both tender and sharp, with a heroine who earns sympathy without losing dignity.
4067-frederick-the-great-and-his-court:
L. Muhlbach's historical romance turns to Frederick the Great and his court, opening on Princess Elizabeth Christine, the neglected royal wife. She waits in her rooms for the prince, whose custom is to give her his arm each morning and lead her to the saloon.

Only then does he speak one word to her, touch her hand, or let her lean on his arm. It is a sweet and sad happiness for a young wife who lives in his light alone. Muhlbach builds court intrigue, war, and marriage around Frederick's cold brilliance. Readers who enjoy long royal romances will find a warm, dramatic life of Prussia's king.
4550-fighting-france-from-dunkerque-to-b:
Edith Wharton wrote Fighting France in 1915, from visits to France during the first year of the First World War. She opens in Paris in August 1914, motoring north from Poitiers past quiet fields and compact grey villages, and she follows the war's shadow across the country. Sections cover the look of Paris, Argonne, Lorraine and the Vosges, the north, Alsace, and the tone of France as a whole.

Wharton reports what she saw and heard: soldiers, refugees, ruined towns, hospitals, and civilians carrying on under strain. The book is eyewitness writing, not a general history of battles, and its strength lies in atmosphere and detail. Readers get a vivid, personal record of France at war, by an American novelist who knew the country well and watched it change month by month.
5321-concerning-the-spiritual-in-art:
Wassily Kandinsky's Concerning the Spiritual in Art, translated by Michael T. H. Sadler, argues that art must serve the spiritual life rather than mere imitation. Its first part treats general aesthetic questions: the movement of the triangle, spiritual revolution, and the pyramid of human progress, while its second part turns to painting itself.

Chapters on the psychological working of colour, the language of form and colour, theory, and art and artists lay out Kandinsky's case for abstract art. The book offers readers a founding text of modern art theory, written by a painter who believed colour and form could speak directly to the soul.
5404-grace-harlowe-s-overland-riders-on-:
Jessie Graham Flower wrote this girls' adventure novel about Grace Harlowe and her friends riding across the American desert. The Overland girls pick ponies for the journey, meet their guide Hi Lang, and watch Grace take on a so-called outlaw pony that no one expects her to ride. Cowboys laugh, then admire her nerve when she stays in the saddle.

Desert camps, a mountain mystery, a Chinese cook's discovery, and a mysterious horseman keep the party on alert as they travel. The story mixes outdoor adventure with friendship and pluck, in the style of early girls' series fiction. Readers get a lively, good-natured western adventure built for young audiences.
6033-petty-troubles-of-married-life-firs:
Honoré de Balzac opens his first part on the petty troubles of married life with a preface in which everyone finds his own impressions of marriage. A friend describes a young woman of good family, well bred, pretty, and worth three hundred thousand in her own right, and a suitor is allowed to approach her.

The mother-in-law praises the girl's susceptibility, fathers discuss five hundred thousand francs and a corner lot, and two hideous notaries, one small and one big, draw the contract. Balzac treats courtship as a negotiation where money, mothers, and manners collide. Small troubles, he shows, begin before the wedding.
6403-petty-troubles-of-married-life-seco:
Honore de Balzac, in the second part of Petty Troubles of Married Life, prefaces his little scenes by doubting whether any author grasps his book's meanings, bearings, or harm. A grocer asks what colour books have, since they are bound in yellow, blue, green, pearl grey, and white. Balzac answers that books are dyed by their authors, some letting colour rub off on others. Books are dark or fair, light brown or red, and they have a sex, male, female, or, sadly, none.

The scenes that follow turn on such petty troubles. A wife, shocked by her husband's excuse that a thing is altogether moral, feels herself a piece of furniture, a block, whose kingdom lies among kitchen utensils. Her vengeance, a listener warns, would lose by being recounted later. Balzac writes marriage as a war of small phrases, where a single excuse can wound more than a quarrel.
7028-the-clicking-of-cuthbert:
Wodehouse's Clicking of Cuthbert is a golf book written, its author jokes, in blood, as the outpouring of a soul seared like a fairway by his iron. It is dedicated to John Henrie and Pat Rogie, jailed at Edinburgh in 1593 for playing golf on the links of Leith every Sabbath during sermon time. Robert Robertson, punished in 1604 for the same reason, shares the honor, and the book cries Fore from the first page.

Wodehouse calls himself a very nearly desperate man, an eighteen handicap golfer slipping toward the twenties. Till now, he says, his cheerful temper, intact heart, and unsoured life handicapped him as a writer, since the public loves a suffering author. The stories that follow turn golfing woe into high comedy for players and non players alike.
7060-at-agincourt:
G A Henty sets At Agincourt in the long and bloody feud between Orleans and Burgundy, which devastated France for years and was not relaxed even before a common enemy. Monstrelet and other contemporary historians record the struggle fully. Henty covers just the opening stretch of that feud, ending with Agincourt, where a small English force defeated the flower of French knighthood.

An illustration shows Guy Aylmer saving the king's life at Agincourt. Apart from Burgundy himself, both sides paused their quarrel briefly, then resumed it even as France remained crushed beneath English power. Henty writes for boys, with feud, battle, and a young hero's courage at the fore, and history kept close to chronicle.
7447-the-rising-of-the-court:
Henry Lawson, the voice of the Australian bush, centers this collection on the courtroom. The scene is dingy and dim, like a well, with a clock high on the wall and a bench gilded like a gingerbread throne. The royal arms hang above, and the witness box stands to one side. In a patch of sunlight sit the ladies of the Prisoners' Aid Society, the one bright spot in a dark and shameful scene.

Only Lawson's prose stories are reproduced here, not his poetry. But the title piece gives the book its mood: a rising of the court where the laws of men count for nothing and spirits go free. The stories that follow show bushmen, workers, and the poor facing judges and the law. Lawson writes with anger and compassion for people the courts process without understanding.
86-a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s:
A Connecticut factory hand wakes in sixth-century England after a blow to the head. Mark Twain's Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur's Court turns Hank Morgan into a court magician at Camelot. He uses modern know-how, from guns to newspapers, to challenge the old order.

Hank befriends King Arthur, reforms knights, and mocks chivalry, church power, and divine right. His eclipse trick wins him fame, but his reforms stir a backlash. The novel ends in war between old and new England. Twain's satire still bites on progress, power, and pride.
8856-the-secrets-of-the-great-city-a-wor:
Edward Winslow Martin exposes the virtues and vices, mysteries, miseries, and crimes of New York City in The Secrets of the Great City. Chapter one describes the city itself, largest and most important in America, its corporate limits embracing Manhattan Island, bounded by the Hudson, East. Harlem rivers and Spuyten Duyvil Creek, almost entirely surrounded by deep water, in sight of the ocean and only sixteen miles from it, naturally the greatest commercial centre.

From that geography, Martin tours police, prisons, gambling dens, dance halls, charities, churches, and slums, in the muckraking manner of the 1860s. The book mixes moral warning with sensational reportage, and it must be read as both. Historians of New York will mine it for street life and social detail. General readers get a lurid, lively guide to a city growing faster than its conscience could follow.
a-connecticut-yankee-in-king-arthur-s-co:
Mark Twain's novel sends a nineteenth-century Connecticut factory man back to the Britain of King Arthur. Twain's preface, dated at Hartford in July 1889, warns that the tale's harsh laws and customs are drawn from real history, if not always from the sixth century itself. The frame story begins at Warwick Castle, where Twain meets the stranger who hands over his manuscript.

The Yankee, Hank Morgan, survives by passing his knowledge off as magic, then sets out to remake Camelot with schools, factories, telephones, and newspapers hidden under the Church's nose. Knights ride out on bicycles, and Arthur tours his kingdom in disguise. Comedy turns darker as reform slides toward war. The book is both a burlesque of chivalric romance and a hard argument about power, superstition, and progress.
a-letter-addressed-to-the-abbe-raynal-on: Thomas Paine writes a letter to the Abbe Raynal on the affairs of North America. He corrects mistakes in Raynal's account of the American Revolution. Paine, secretary for foreign affairs to Congress during the war, writes as author of Common Sense. The letter defends the American cause against French misunderstanding.
a-passion-in-the-desert:
Honoré de Balzac frames his tale at a Paris menagerie, where a lady marvels at a showman working with a hyena. Ernest Dowson translated the story. The narrator answers her wonder with a tale told him by an old soldier who had lost a leg. In Egypt, that soldier had been lost alone in the desert.

There, starving and afraid, the soldier found a panther, and the two formed a strange, tender bond built on food, trust, and loneliness. He came to love the animal and to fear it in the same hour. The ending, when rescue approaches, is sudden and sad. Balzac makes the desert itself a character in a few pages.
art: Clive Bell asks what art is, and answers with an aesthetic hypothesis built on significant form rather than story or likeness. He tests that idea against post impressionism, religion, history, and ethics, then traces Christian art from rise to decline and classical revival. Later chapters praise Cezanne, simplification, and design, and they look ahead to art in society. Bell writes with bold, brisk confidence, and the book helped shape modern talk about painting.
at-agincourt:
G. A. Henty's At Agincourt follows the early struggle between the houses of Orleans and Burgundy up to Henry the Fifth's astonishing victory. Henty draws on Monstrelet and other contemporary historians for the long, bloody feud that devastated France and destroyed life and property.

At Agincourt a handful of Englishmen beat the chivalry of France, and the two French factions laid aside their differences for a moment, only to renew them while France lay prostrate. Henty's young hero Guy Aylmer, pictured saving the king's life, carries the reader through the campaign. Boys and general readers of historical adventure will find the feud, the marches and the battle vividly told.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adalbert:
Adalbert, Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen, was born about 1000 and died at Goslar in 1072, son of Count Friedrich von Goseck, with Agnes of Weimar lineage. He rose through canon at Halberstadt, subdeacon to Hamburg's archbishop, and provost of Halberstadt Cathedral, to Archbishop of Hamburg in 1043 or 1045 by royal appointment. His province covered the Scandinavian peninsula, much of the Wend lands, and territory north of the Elbe.

At the outset he took up Hamburg's old feud with the Billings, with Henry III's cooperation, campaigned with the emperor against the Liutzi, and journeyed with him to Rome in 1046. When Henry wished to make him pope after settling the papal schism, Adalbert refused and proposed his friend Suidger, later Clement II. He aided Wend conversion, raised three bishoprics, and dreamed of a northern patriarchate at Hamburg, but pride, Adam of Bremen notes, marred a generous and zealous character.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adrian-willae:
Adrian Willaert was a composer and founder of the Venetian school, born at Bruges, or by other accounts Roulers, between 1480 and 1490, who died at Venice on 7 December 1562. Taught in Paris by Jean Moulin, a disciple of Josquin, he went first to Rome in 1516, then to Ferrara, joining King Louis II of Bohemia and Hungary's service. On 12 December 1527 he became choir master of St. Mark's at Venice.

Though grounded in counterpoint, Willaert fell under the new Italian tendency to let harmony predominate over melody. St. Mark's had two choir lofts, one each side of the main altar, each with an organ. Willaert split the choir in two, using the sections antiphonally or together, and composed psalms and other works for alternating double choirs. The innovation met instant success and shaped the new method. His disciples, including Ciprian de Rore and the Gabrielis, formed the Venetian school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrose-autpe:
Ambrose Autpert, early medieval Benedictine writer and abbot, was born in France early in the eighth century. He died after little more than a year's abbacy at St. Vincent on the Volturno near Beneventum in 778 or 779. Forgotten today, he had a name in his own century: Charlemagne used his talents, Stephen IV protected him, and his monastery ranked among Italy's great houses. He is sometimes confused with a later Autpert, Monte Cassino abbot and author of sermons and a spiritual treatise.

His chief work is the Expositio in Apocalypsim, a commentary on Revelation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-animals-in-ch:
In Christian art, animals occupy a far greater place than in pagan art. In early Latin and Byzantine Christianity, and in its medieval bloom, animals abound in sculpture, manuscripts, stained glass, and tapestry. Three reasons explain this fondness. First, animals symbolize a virtue or vice usually attributed to them. Second, animal forms served as decoration. Third, medieval designers returned to studying nature, embracing man, animals, and plants.

Early paintings show dragons, human-headed birds, and winged lions, until wars and iconoclasm ended this art. Romanesque buildings brought fantastic types, with monsters fighting one another. Around the glorified Christ, the lion, ox, man, and eagle hold holy books. French gargoyles, no two alike, seem copies of nature. Symbolism comes mostly from bestiaries: the lion for strength and courage; the siren for voluptuousness; the pelican for charity. The four Evangelist animals characterize the Evangelists, and saints are accompanied by animals.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anselm-eckart:
Anselm Eckart, missionary, born at Bingen in 1721, died at Polotsk in 1809. Entering the Jesuits at nineteen, he went to Brazil. Two years after his arrival, he and his brethren were seized and carried to Portugal, languishing in prison till death or the king's summons released them. Eckart was confined eighteen years in Almeida and St. Julian dungeons. He wrote of his and his companions' prison sufferings.

Upon Joseph I's death in 1777, Pombal fell, and surviving victims were released. The Society, suppressed four years earlier, had continued in Russia. Eckart applied for readmission, and for thirty-two years wore the proscribed habit. After serving as novice master at Dünaburg, he was sent to Polotsk. There this venerable confessor, perhaps Pombal's last survivor, preserved in extreme old age the vigour that had sustained him in missions and captivity. He died in his eighty-eighth year, the sixty-ninth after admission.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-shert: Blessed John Shert, a martyr, was a Cheshire man who took his B.A. at Brasenose College, Oxford, in 1566. After work as a London schoolmaster and in Dr. Thomas Stapleton's service at Douai, he joined the seminary in 1576, later taking priestly orders through the English College at Rome, its senior scholar among the first six. He left Reims for England in August 1579 and was sent to the Tower in July 1581.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-william-ha: Blessed William Hart, a martyr, was born at Wells in 1558 and suffered at York on 15 March 1583. Trappes Scholar at Lincoln College, Oxford, in 1571, he followed his rector to Douai, took the college oath at Rome in 1579, and was ordained priest. Returning to England in 1581, he laboured in Yorkshire and was present at the Mass where Blessed William Lacy was captured, before his own arrest and execution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blaise-gisber:
Blaise Gisbert, a French Jesuit rhetorician and critic, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry.
